title: CIA Director Ratcliffe Makes Unannounced Trip to Moscow
dek: John Ratcliffe, director of the Central Intelligence Agency, flew to Moscow on a U.S. military aircraft over the weekend, according to reporting by NBC News, ABC News, BBC News, and other outlets. The purpose and participants of the talks remain unconfirmed. The trip marks the first known visit to Russia by Ratcliffe in his role as CIA director.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: A U.S. military C-17 Globemaster transport aircraft departed Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Sunday, landed in Moscow at Vnukovo International Airport on Tuesday morning, and departed Tuesday afternoon, according to FlightRadar24 tracking data and reporting by multiple news outlets.
bottom_line: Both Washington and Moscow have declined to confirm the purpose or participants in Ratcliffe's talks, leaving the agenda and outcomes unverified. The identity of his interlocutors, the topics discussed, and any agreements or understandings reached remain unconfirmed by official sources.
body: John Ratcliffe, director of the Central Intelligence Agency, flew unannounced to Moscow to hold talks, according to reporting by NBC News, ABC News, BBC News, and other outlets. The visit represents a rare high-level engagement between U.S. and Russian officials during a period of strained relations.

According to NBC News, a U.S. military transport aircraft landed at Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow on Tuesday morning. FlightRadar24 tracking data showed the plane, a Boeing C-17 Globemaster III, departed from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Sunday just before 5 p.m. ET, landed in Riga, Latvia, and then proceeded to Moscow, arriving just after 10 a.m. local time. The aircraft departed Moscow on Tuesday afternoon, according to flight radar data reported by NBC News and BBC News.

Neither the CIA nor the U.S. military responded immediately to questions about the mission. When asked about the aircraft, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told NBC News he did not have information about it. The White House, U.S. Embassy in Moscow, and Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to inquiries. The source of the reporting declined to say whom Ratcliffe was meeting with or what was the focus of the talks, according to NBC News.

CIA directors have historically served as presidential envoys in high-stakes talks with adversaries. According to NBC News, former President Joe Biden turned to then-CIA Director William Burns to relay stern warnings to Russia before and after President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ratcliffe has made other trips to adversarial or complex diplomatic settings: per NBC News, he visited Venezuela in January to meet with interim President Delcy Rodríguez about two weeks after the U.S. military seized President Nicolás Maduro in a raid in Caracas, and traveled to Cuba in May to meet with government leaders, making him the highest-ranking Trump administration official to visit the island.

The visit appears to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, though the BBC reported he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow. John Foreman, who served as a British military attaché to Moscow from 2019 to 2022, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the timing and secrecy of the visit suggest high-stakes discussions. "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up," Foreman said, per BBC News.

Foreman suggested the trip could concern escalation management given speculation about recent drone activity in Germany potentially linked to Russia, or the release of U.S. detainees held in Russia. Ratcliffe played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine, according to BBC News. The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, former U.S. marine Paul Whelan, and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva, the BBC reported.
